notes.h: What a mould is (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Moulds are one of the micro-organisms that spoil food. Knowing what kind of living thing a mould is explains how it feeds and why it grows where it does.
points: Moulds are multicellular, filamentous fungi: their bodies are made of many cells joined in thread-like filaments.
Moulds are not plants because they have no chlorophyll (the green pigment plants use to make their own food), and they are not bacteria.

Moulds are saprophytes, which means they feed on dead organic matter such as bread, cheese, jam, fruit and decaying plant material. They digest it outside their bodies and then absorb the digested products.
notes.tip: Moulds and yeasts are both fungi, but bacteria are not fungi. Fungi are eukaryotic (their cells have a nucleus) and bacteria are prokaryotic (no nucleus), a contrast short questions use.

notes.h: Structure of a mould (Higher Level only)
notes.b: A mould's visible body is built from thread-like filaments. Each part has a name and a job, and the parts are the labels exams ask for on a diagram.
points: Hyphae (singular hypha): thread-like filaments that grow over and into the food and absorb its nutrients, which is how the mould feeds.
Mycelium: the interwoven mass of hyphae that forms the visible growth, such as the fluffy or powdery layer on bread.
Sporangiophore: an upright hypha that rises from the mycelium and carries a sporangium at its tip, lifting the spores up so they can escape into the air.
Sporangium: a round, spore-filled case at the tip of a sporangiophore; it bursts open when ripe and releases spores into the air.
Conidia: in Penicillium, and also in Aspergillus, spores are borne in chains at the tips of branched conidiophores (spore-bearing hyphae) instead of inside a round sporangium.

Diagram: a mould growing on a food surface, showing the mycelium spreading across the food, a sporangiophore rising from it and a sporangium at its tip; label hypha, mycelium, sporangiophore and sporangium.
notes.tip: Diagram questions on a mould ask you to label the sporangium, the hypha or sporangiophore, and the mycelium. They are short questions worth about 2 marks per label.

notes.h: Habitat and sources of moulds (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Mould spores are almost everywhere, which is why food left out so often goes mouldy. Knowing where they come from shows how they reach food.
points: Moulds are saprophytes: they feed on dead organic matter, so they grow on decaying food and plant material.
Spores are carried in the air, on dust, on food packaging and on unclean utensils, and they settle on food.
Soil and damp indoor surfaces act as reservoirs (stores) from which spores spread to food.
Already-mouldy food is also a source: a mouldy item releases spores that spread to food stored beside it.
Rhizopus is the common bread mould; it grows on bread, fruit and other moist starchy or sugary foods.

notes.h: Conditions for mould growth (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Mould spores only grow into a mould when six conditions are met. Each one gives a way to stop growth, and each has a reason you can give.
points: Food: moulds feed on the organic matter in food, such as bread, cheese, jam and fruit.
Warmth: most moulds are mesophiles (they prefer moderate temperatures); Penicillium grows best at 20 to 25 °C, and cold slows growth.
Moisture: moulds need moisture to grow, so frozen and very dry foods are less at risk.
Oxygen: moulds are aerobic (they need oxygen), so they grow on the surface of food, such as jam, or through open-textured foods such as bread.
pH: moulds prefer slightly acidic conditions, around pH 4 to 6; strong acids inhibit their growth.
Time: moulds need about 24 to 48 hours to establish visible growth, because the spores must germinate and the mycelium must spread.
Freezing at −18 °C inactivates mould growth, but it does not kill the mould, so growth can start again after thawing.
notes.tip: Exams ask for four or five conditions: name each one and give its reason, for example moisture needed so frozen and very dry foods are less at risk. Never write that freezing kills mould; it only inactivates growth.

notes.b: One type of mould is often asked about in detail. Penicillium is a good choice because its features are easy to remember.
points: Penicillium is a saprophytic mould with a green-blue, powdery appearance, which comes from its chains of conidia.
It grows on bread, jam, cheese and fruit, and favours temperatures of 20 to 25 °C.
Penicillium reproduces asexually only, by conidia, so it never forms a zygospore.
Heat above 75 °C destroys Penicillium, whereas freezing only inactivates its growth.
notes.tip: An account of one mould needs its name, description, conditions and reproduction. Reproduction carries the most marks, so describe spore release and germination. Green-blue and powdery is Penicillium; do not mix in features of other moulds.

notes.h: Rhizopus, Mucor and Aspergillus (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Other moulds can be given as your named example. Their differences are in colour, spore structure and whether they reproduce sexually.
points: Rhizopus (the black bread mould) is saprophytic, with fluffy white mycelium and black pin-head sporangia that hold its spores.
Rhizopus reproduces both sexually and asexually, so it can form a zygospore as well as spores.
Mucor is saprophytic, with white hyphae and grey sporangia, and reproduces both sexually and asexually.
Aspergillus is saprophytic and black or green; it favours 20 to 25 °C and reproduces asexually only, by conidia.
notes.tip: Black pin-head sporangia means Rhizopus, not Penicillium. Rhizopus and Mucor use both kinds of reproduction, while Penicillium and Aspergillus are asexual only.

notes.b: Moulds reproduce by releasing spores, tiny cells that spread through the air. Some moulds can also reproduce sexually, which gives a tough resting stage.
points: Asexual reproduction, first stage: once the mycelium is established, a hypha (the sporangiophore) grows upwards and its head forms a sporangium, or in some moulds chains of conidia.
When the sporangium ripens it bursts, releasing spores into the air, so they travel to new food.
A spore that lands on suitable food germinates (starts to grow) and develops a new mycelium.
Sexual reproduction (Rhizopus and Mucor): two compatible hyphae grow beside each other and fuse.
The dividing wall between the fused hyphae breaks down and a thick-walled zygospore forms.
The zygospore protects the spores until conditions are suitable; then it germinates, hyphae grow out and spores are released.
notes.tip: Reproduction carries the most marks in an account of one mould. Describe sporangium or conidia release and germination, and add the zygospore only if the mould reproduces sexually. Never give Penicillium a zygospore.

notes.h: Structure of a yeast cell (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Yeasts are single-celled fungi. Each cell is a single oval or round unit, larger and more regular in shape than a bacterium.
points: Yeast is a eukaryote, meaning its cell has a true nucleus; it is a fungus, not a bacterium.
Cell wall: a rigid outer layer that gives the cell its shape, so it holds together, and protects it.
Cell membrane: a thin layer inside the cell wall that controls which substances pass in and out, so the cell takes in food and keeps unwanted substances out.
Nucleus: a membrane-bound structure containing the genetic material, so the cell is a eukaryote, for example unlike a bacterium.
Vacuole: a fluid-filled storage space within the cytoplasm.
Granular cytoplasm: the jelly-like contents of the cell, containing food reserves stored as granules.
Diagram: a yeast cell labelled cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus, vacuole and granular cytoplasm.
notes.tip: Yeast diagrams ask for the vacuole, nucleus and granular cytoplasm (food reserve). Do not describe yeast as a bacterium, and do not give it spores or hyphae.

notes.h: Habitat, growth and reproduction of yeasts (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Yeasts live wherever sugar and moisture are found. They reproduce in a different way from moulds, by budding rather than by spores.
points: Yeasts occur naturally on the skins of fruit, especially grapes, and in soil, in the air, on plant surfaces and on sugary foods.
Yeasts need sugar as food, moisture, warmth and time to grow.
Yeast is facultative, meaning it can do either: it respires with oxygen, or ferments sugar when oxygen is absent.
In fermentation, yeast converts sugar into carbon dioxide and alcohol.
Reproduction is asexual, by budding: a small bud grows from the parent cell, enlarges and breaks away as a new cell.
Yeast spoils sugary foods such as juices, jam and syrups by fermenting them. Baker's and brewer's yeast is Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
notes.tip: Short questions ask you to contrast budding with spore release: yeast buds, moulds make spores. Do not write that yeast is anaerobic.

notes.h: Structure of a bacterial cell (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Bacteria are prokaryotes: single cells with no true nucleus, so their genetic material lies free in the cytoplasm. This is the main contrast with fungi, whose cells have a nucleus.
points: Cell wall: a rigid layer, made of peptidoglycan, that gives the bacterial cell its shape and protects it.
Cell membrane: controls the movement of substances in and out of the cell.
Cytoplasm: the jelly-like interior where the cell's chemical reactions take place.
Ribosomes: small structures in the cytoplasm where proteins are made, so the cell can build and repair itself.
Flagella: whip-like tails that rotate to move the bacterium; not all bacteria have them.
Nucleoid: the region containing the single circular loop of DNA, lying free in the cytoplasm; plasmids are small extra loops of DNA.
Bacteria reproduce asexually by binary fission, where one cell divides in two; under ideal conditions some divide about every 20 minutes.
Diagram: a bacterial cell labelled cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, flagella and nucleoid.
notes.tip: Bacterial cell diagrams ask for the ribosomes, flagella and cytoplasm. Short questions also ask you to compare fungi and bacteria: fungi have a nucleus, bacteria do not.

keyTerms.definition: Thread-like filaments that make up the body of a mould and absorb nutrients from food.
The interwoven mass of hyphae that forms the visible growth of a mould.
A round, spore-filled case at the tip of a sporangiophore that bursts open to release spores.
A thick-walled structure formed in sexual reproduction of a mould, which protects spores until conditions are suitable.
An organism that feeds on dead organic matter.
Asexual reproduction in yeast in which a small bud grows from the parent cell and separates as a new cell.
Spores formed in chains at the tips of branched conidiophores, as in Penicillium.
A single-celled organism, such as a bacterium, with no membrane-bound nucleus.
Whip-like structures that rotate to propel a bacterium.
The region of a bacterial cell that holds its single circular loop of DNA.

factCards.term: Six conditions needed for mould growth
factCards.definition: Food, warmth, moisture, oxygen, a slightly acidic pH and time.
A sporangiophore forms a sporangium, which bursts when ripe and releases spores; a spore landing on suitable food grows a new mycelium.
Two compatible hyphae fuse, the dividing wall breaks down, a zygospore forms, and it later germinates to release spores.

factCards.term: Penicillium: favoured temperature and what destroys it
factCards.definition: It favours 20 to 25 °C and is destroyed by heat above 75 °C.
Cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus, vacuole and granular cytoplasm.
Cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, flagella and nucleoid.
Asexually, by budding, in which a bud grows from the parent cell and separates.
Carbon dioxide and alcohol, formed when yeast converts sugar in the absence of oxygen.

questions.prompt: Identify two structures of a mould and state the function of each.
questions.model: Hyphae: thread-like filaments that grow into the food and absorb its nutrients. Mycelium: the network of hyphae that forms the visible growth on the food. Accept also sporangium, a spore-filled case that bursts to release spores, and sporangiophore, the upright hypha that carries the sporangium. Award one mark for each correctly named structure and one for each correct function, up to six.

questions.prompt: Explain how temperature and moisture affect the growth of moulds on stored food. Refer to a named mould in your answer.
questions.model: Named mould: Penicillium, a saprophytic blue-green mould found on bread, jam, cheese and fruit. Temperature: most moulds are mesophiles; Penicillium grows best at 20 to 25 °C. Warm conditions speed up growth and reproduction, so food left at room temperature becomes mouldy quickly. Freezing at −18 °C inactivates growth, and temperatures above 75 °C destroy the mould. Moisture: moulds need moisture to grow and absorb nutrients; food with high moisture content is at greater risk, while dry foods support little growth. Freezing makes water unavailable, so frozen foods are unsuitable for mould growth. Reproduction: the mould forms spores that are released into the air and settle on food; a spore landing on moist, warm food germinates and grows a mycelium within 24 to 48 hours. Award marks for a clear named mould, the effect of each factor with a reason, and an example of stored food.
